_comment: Declared mutants. Each entry names one behaviour change and the single test
that must catch it; scripts/check-mutants.py requires the test to pass
Rules for an entry. The mutation must change behaviour, not well-formedness:
neutering a guard so the code below it runs on undefined state makes the
failure a property of the nonsense rather than of the line. It must occur
exactly once in the file. 'why' states the defect the line prevents, so a
reader can judge whether the test is pinning the right thing.
Entries naming a file a branch does not carry are skipped, not failed: each
branch adds the entries for the mechanism it introduces.

mutants.why: An output the node has not buried to the required depth must not be credited, and the disagreement with the indexer must alarm. Without this the exchange credits a deposit a reorganisation can still take back.
A coinbase output is real but unspendable until maturity. Crediting it early hands out a balance the node will refuse to spend, and it is not an indexer disagreement, so it must not alarm either.

An entry is final only when the node has buried the outpoint past MaxReorgDepth. The Ledger contract says Pending may leave out swept outputs, so 'credited and not pending' is not finality: without the depth test a swept credit inside the horizon is recorded final and a reversal after a reorganisation is never re-credited.

A reconcile tick that lands during a backoff must be deferred and made up, not dropped. The full pass is the only safety net against a notification the server never sent, so dropping the tick lets one permanently refused address starve it for the life of the process.

Only two reply timeouts in a row may rebuild the connection. A reply that arrived, even an error, breaks the run; without the reset a timeout, one refused address and another timeout rebuild a healthy connection.

An address that leaves the tracked set must leave the money views with it. The UTXO cache is what GetBalance, GetAllUTXOs and the selector read, so an unpruned entry keeps a retired address's coins spendable.
A listunspent already in flight when TrackAddresses drops its address must not commit, or it undoes the pruning above and makes the output selectable again.

The lying broadcaster must hand the engine a txid that is not the real one. Replacing the first character with a fixed 'f' returns the input unchanged for the one real txid in sixteen that already starts with 'f', and scenario 8 then fails, because it requires a node txid that differs from the engine's own and was handed two that are equal. A spurious failure in one run in sixteen, not a vacuous pass.

Two refreshes of one address can be in flight at once and their replies can arrive in either order. Without the ticket order the older reply commits last, and because the merge drops every output its own reply does not list, a deposit the newer reply found leaves the cache while the record dates the set current.

mutants.replace: if live := c.liveGen.Load(); gen != live && false {
mutants.why: A headers reply buffered on a connection that has since been replaced still answers its caller. Recording its tip moves the height backwards, past the newer one the replacing connection recorded in its handshake.

The pass that follows the first ping timeout has nothing to refresh whenever no address has a change pending. Counted as a clean pass it resets the reply-timeout count, so the second timeout counts as the first and a server that has stopped answering while holding the connection open is never replaced.

mutants.replace: if live := c.liveGen.Load(); gen != live && false {
mutants.why: A subscribe reply from a connection that has been replaced records a status that was true when the server wrote it and dates the address's freshness now, on a connection that carries no subscription for it.

A write that fails on a live context means the socket is gone and dropLocked has forgotten it. Reported as a plain error the refresher classifies it as one the server chose to send, which never rebuilds the connection, and waits out a backoff before finding out through the next call.

Version 2 takes the Argon2id parameters from the file, so a file written with a weak work factor opens as readily as a strong one unless a floor refuses it. Not an edit: editing the parameters changes the derived key and the file stops opening. What is caught is a keystore legitimately created weak, by an older writer or another implementation, whose holder would never learn that its at-rest protection is worth much less than they believe.

The header is plaintext beside the ciphertext and is bound into the AEAD so that an edit to it is a forgery. Every individual field has a second guard, so removing the binding shows up nowhere in the refusals; what is lost is the property itself, that the file authenticates its own header rather than depending on five separate checks all remaining in place.
Version 1 files were sealed with no additional data. Opening one with version 2's bound header makes every keystore written before v0.4 unreadable, which is the loss of the keys in it.

The file records which key source wrote it, and a manager's source is fixed at construction. Without the comparison, a manager holding a Vault key pointed at a passphrase keystore runs Argon2id over an empty passphrase, and the reverse runs HKDF over an empty key; both report a decryption failure and send an operator to look for a wrong passphrase that was never used.

mutants.find: return hkdf.Key(sha256.New, m.extKey, ks.Salt, hkdfInfo, encKeySize)
mutants.replace: return hkdf.Key(sha256.New, m.extKey, nil, hkdfInfo, encKeySize)
mutants.why: An external key does not change between saves. The salt is what makes the AES key differ each time; without it every save of that keystore uses one key, and a 96-bit random nonce carries the whole requirement that no two saves repeat.

The header check runs on the way out as well as on the way in, so this package cannot write a file it would refuse to read. Without that, a writer and a reader that disagree produce a keystore nothing opens, and the disagreement surfaces on the next process start rather than at the save.

The unencrypted public key list is what an operator or an external tool reads to find the address to send to. Version 2 binds it into the AEAD, but version 1 bound nothing, so this comparison against the decrypted records is the only thing that refuses a swapped address in a version 1 file, and a withdrawal goes to whoever edited it.

What the AEAD binds is the canonical re-encoding of the fields this build knows. A field it does not know would be dropped on the way in and never authenticated, so the file would carry content the header's tamper-evidence does not cover.

A json.Decoder reads one value and ignores whatever follows it, where json.Unmarshal refuses it. Without this the refusal of unknown fields covers only the inside of the object, and bytes appended to the file sit outside everything the header's tamper-evidence covers.

Go's decoder keeps the last of two members with the same name, and headerAAD authenticates what the decoder kept. A copy of pubkeys prepended before the real one therefore loads cleanly and is authenticated away, while a reader that takes the first member sees the address the person who edited the file chose.

Save writes the manager's keys over whatever is at the path. Without this test a manager that never read the file replaces the keys in it with its own, which is none on a manager that has only just opened, and returns no error. The keystore is still a keystore afterwards, so nothing downstream reports anything either.

The bit that lets Save overwrite is set where a load succeeds, not where the file is read. A load that got the bytes and then failed to decrypt them knows less about the keystore than one that never opened it, and it is the state an operator retries from. Setting it on the read lets that manager write an empty keystore over a populated one, which is the defect the guard exists for.

The push scenarios believe the fake indexer, so it has to answer every method electrumx.Client sends. A method the client sends and the fake does not answer meets 'unknown method', which the client reads as an error from the server, so a scenario reaching that path takes the error branch and reports success without exercising what it names. A double that has drifted from its client is worse than no double, because it is believed.

mutants.replace: var forwarders = map[string]bool{"Call": true, "call": true, "callGen": true}
mutants.why: The forwarder skip drops a whole function body. Only Call and call forward a method parameter to another caller; callGen and callLocked go to sendLocked and await, so skipping either hides every real call site in its body and the fake can fall behind the client with the coverage test green.
The forwarder skip is keyed on the receiver type as well as the method name. Without the receiver test, any method called call or Call on any type in the package hides every call site in its body.
Every declaration is walked, not only the function declarations: a package-level function literal lives in a GenDecl, and a reading that filters to FuncDecl never sees the call sites inside one.

A client cannot change network once addresses are tracked: the UTXO cache, the subscriptions and every script hash were derived under the old prefix, so it would be asking one network's server about another network's keys and answering 'no coins' for every address.

A write that failed after the rename left the new record in the file. Rolling the map back there makes memory contradict the file, and because every Put writes the whole file from memory the next one puts the older record back over the newer: a Built intent, with a signed transaction and reserved inputs, silently reverts.

The snapshot is the signer's whole view of the chain and it has no other way to check it. An old one lists outputs that may already be spent, so building from it signs a second transaction over inputs the first one used.

The intent id is chosen by the system that asks for the withdrawal and it becomes a file name. Unchecked, a separator or a parent reference writes the record outside the store, or reads another file as a withdrawal.

A save that landed and is only unconfirmed for durability leaves the record in the store, where Recover and any broadcaster will find it Built. Treating that as unsaved releases the inputs of a signed transaction, and the next withdrawal selects them: two transactions stand over one input and one is rejected for good.

A reservation expires by its TTL and is dropped when the set is loaded, and a signer on a new host has no set at all, so a signed withdrawal waiting for the broadcaster can have no reservation in this process. Its inputs are still unspent and therefore in the snapshot, so the pass over the store's Built withdrawals is the only thing keeping the next selection off them.

A case-folding filesystem answers a read of W1.json with w1.json. Without this check the store reports one withdrawal as another, so Submit takes the second as already submitted, its request is moved aside and it is never paid.

Recover re-sends built withdrawals in the order List returns, oldest first, as withdraw.FileStore does. Without the sort the order is whatever the directory read gives, so the oldest signed transaction is not the first one re-sent after a restart. The first version of the test asserted an order the directory read already produced, so it passed with the sort deleted.

TrackAddresses reads the prefix, validates the addresses against it, then commits. A SetHRP that lands in between is silently overwritten without this test, and both calls return nil: the client then tracks one network's addresses while another is pinned, which is the mainnet-reading-stagenet case pinning exists to prevent.

A node that answers zero for the tip has no chain to speak of. Writing the snapshot anyway leaves a file the signer refuses as self-contradicting, so every withdrawal stops until a good snapshot replaces it, and the signer cannot tell that state from a watcher that has not started.

A file name and the id inside it can agree and both still be unusable. Without the check List hands the engine a withdrawal that Get and Put refuse, so its next transition cannot be saved and the record is stuck wherever the engine left it.

The fee of an ML-DSA payment is dominated by its inputs, so a selection made under a one-input target and answered with three is short of its own fee. Accepting it signs a transaction the node refuses for paying less than its weight.

Build's first state check reads the caller's copy of the intent, which another worker can have advanced between its read and this lock. Without the stored state deciding, two workers each holding a Created copy of one intent both build, each reserving different inputs because the other's are taken, and each broadcasts. The recipient is paid twice from different inputs, which is the first of the two failure modes the package exists to prevent.

Failed is terminal and nothing was sent, but Submit answers the same id with no error, so an exchange retrying a payout reaches Process again. Without this branch Process returns a nil error and an empty txid, so the caller records the withdrawal as sent and a circuit breaker fed that nil records a success.

mutants.find:
note(fmt.Errorf("recover %s: not sent: %w", in.ID, err))
			continue
mutants.replace:
note(fmt.Errorf("recover %s: not sent: %w", in.ID, err))
			break
mutants.why: The context stops Recover's sending, not its re-reserving. Breaking here leaves every Built intent after the first one unreserved, and their inputs belong to signed transactions that may be in a mempool, so the next selection can take them.

A fee target under the real vsize makes selectForFee accept a selection that cannot pay its own fee. BuildSendTransaction then computes a negative change and returns ErrInsufficientFunds, which is neither transient nor a context error, so the engine fails the withdrawal permanently. The measured figure is 976 vB per further input and the guide's size table gives it; 950 was short from three inputs up.

mutants.find: ErrFailed = fmt.Errorf("withdraw: intent failed permanently (%w)", rpc.ErrPermanent)
mutants.why: One withdrawal that cannot succeed says nothing about the node or the indexer. resilience.CircuitBreaker recognises a per-request fault by rpc.ErrPermanent and counts anything else as systemic, so an ErrFailed that wraps nothing makes three retries of one bad payout open the breaker and stop every withdrawal for its cooldown. That is the outcome the breaker's own documentation says it exists to prevent.

A withdrawal the engine refuses to act on is a fact about that withdrawal. The breaker counts every error it does not recognise as systemic, and Process returns ErrWrongState to the worker that loses the build race for an id, which a worker pool does as a matter of course: three losses in a row then open the breaker and stop every withdrawal for its cooldown. That is the outcome the breaker's own documentation says it exists to prevent, and it is the defect ErrFailed had in the first round of this branch. ErrHeld and ErrReservationLost are deliberately not in the set, because each is a transaction an operator must resolve before anything else is sent.

Re-reserving the Built intents is a repair of the spent set, not a network call, and it cannot happen unless the List that finds them answers. A store that bounds its queries with the context, which is what the guide tells an exchange to implement over its database, answers an ended context with an error; Recover would then return before the loop and leave every Built intent unreserved, with its inputs selectable while its signed bytes may be in a mempool. Both in-tree stores ignore the context, so only a context-bound store shows it.

The fee target must size the inputs the selection takes, not the candidate list it chose from. Budgeting for every candidate charges a further 976 vB for each output the payment will not spend and counts the first input twice, so a wallet holding its coins in one output is asked for 2,076 vB of headroom against a transaction of about 1,073 and the selector refuses a payment the wallet can pay. This is the program that produces the stagenet verification transaction, where one freshly funded output is the ordinary case.

A fee target under the real vsize makes the selection accept inputs that cannot pay their own fee. BuildSendTransaction then computes a negative change and returns ErrInsufficientFunds, which is neither transient nor a context error, so the engine fails the withdrawal permanently. The measured figure is 976 vB per further input; 950 was short from three inputs up. The constant now appears in this example and in the split signer, so each is pinned where it stands.

A script hash carries nothing about which chain its script belongs to, so a server indexing another chain answers listunspent with a well-formed empty list. Without the gate on the call, a client that connected before its network prefix was known is never verified at all: it reports no deposits for the life of the process, records every pass as successful, and the reconciler compares an empty cache against an empty answer and finds no mismatch.
The recorded verification is true of one connection to one server. Keyed by the prefix alone it would carry over to a connection that was never verified, which is a verdict about a different server.

An output with a nil script serialises as 9 bytes where a witness v5 or v7 program serialises as 43. A fee measured over empty placeholders is under the minimum relay rate for the transaction actually broadcast, so the mint is signed and not relayed.
checkFee is what refuses a rate above MaxFeeRateShorsPerVB and a fee above MaxFeeShors. Without it a fee-rate typo is paid, and docs/SECURITY.md tells the reader the builders cap both.

Submit's registration is one Create, and the store's refusal of an id it holds is the only thing between a client retry under an idempotency key and a second record for the same withdrawal. Without it the retry's write lands as Created over the record a worker has driven to Built or Broadcast, and the next Process builds a second transaction from other inputs and pays the recipient twice.

Update writes only over the state the caller read. Without the check a writer holding a copy the store has moved past puts the record back: Created over Built, Broadcast over Confirmed. The engine re-reads under its lock inside one process, so this check is what refuses a second process, or a caller of the store itself, that skipped the re-read.

Broadcast's first check reads the caller's copy, which another worker can have sent between the caller's read and the lock. Without the stored record deciding, the second worker sends the same bytes, its lost reply renews a reservation over inputs the first marked spent, and its save of Built over the first's Broadcast is refused by the store as stale, so the payout is reported as an error and the breaker is fed for a transaction that went out once.

UpdateConfirmations acts on the stored record. Without the re-read a loop holding a copy from one block earlier writes Broadcast over a record another loop has confirmed; the store refuses the write as stale and the loop reports an error for an intent that is complete, and a ledger acting on the Confirmed transition cannot rely on seeing it once.

A permanent rejection releases the intent's inputs and records it Failed. Released first, a failed save leaves the store holding a Built intent with signed bytes whose inputs the next withdrawal can select; Recover then re-reserves them against that withdrawal and reports a conflict. Saved first, a failed save leaves the intent as it was, inputs held, and the next attempt reaches the same verdict.

A retry after a lost reply renews the reservation of a Built intent. When an earlier attempt succeeded and its record did not land, the set holds the intent's own inputs as sent, and refusing them names a conflicting withdrawal that does not exist: the engine reports ErrReservationLost, which the guide says halts every payout, for a transaction that went out once.

An entry that records a send is permanent until the chain confirms it. Accepting the intent's own sent entry and then writing a reservation over it gives the inputs of a transaction in a mempool an expiry, after which the next withdrawal selects them and double-spends its own payment.

The re-read decides what the engine may do and is not a network call. Bound to the caller's context, a store that honours the context answers an ended one with an error, and Broadcast returns before it renews the reservation or records the attempt; a worker pool whose per-task deadlines expire while tasks wait then never renews, the reservation lapses at its TTL, and the inputs of a signed transaction are selected by the next withdrawal. The same context ending a moment later, inside the send, is a lost reply that does both.

Broadcast is the one place a send starts, and the shipped broadcaster lists every Built intent each pass and sends each. A Built intent whose inputs another withdrawal holds is two signed transactions over one input; refusing it only in Recover leaves the next pass to send it, and the second send also overwrites the first transaction's record of the shared input in the spent set.

MarkBroadcast writes entries with no withdrawal id, and the pool payout and consolidation examples use it. A Reserve that names no withdrawal would match those entries as its own, skip every write, and answer nil: the caller is told the inputs are reserved for it while the set records them as spent in a transaction that is out.

Create is the registration write, and its refusal of an id the store holds is what keeps a second Submit of one id from writing Created over the record a worker has driven to Built or Broadcast. The in-memory store has the same check pinned separately; this is the file-backed one an exchange without a database runs.

Update writes only over the state the caller read. In the shared directory the three processes hold no common lock, so this comparison is the only thing that refuses a process writing over a record another process has moved, and without it a late write puts a sent intent back to Built or a built one back to Created.

A rejection on the attempt after a lost reply must hold the intent. Failing it releases inputs the first transmission may still spend: peers keep a relayed transaction for the mempool expiry and can mine it after the node forgot it, and the exchange then pays the recipient again from other coins.

The mark that peers may hold the bytes is written before the send, so a save that fails after the send cannot lose it. Without it a rejection on the next attempt fails the intent and releases inputs the first transmission may still spend.

A held intent is never sent again. Once the node has the payment under another txid, or under this one after a rejection, a re-send answers "already in chain" and the intent would become a Broadcast intent whose record disagrees with the network.
Abandon frees inputs whose transaction peers may still hold. The wait is the node's mempool expiry; freeing them earlier lets a second withdrawal spend inputs the first can still take.
A transaction the node knows is in its mempool or its chain. Abandoning it frees inputs that are spent, and marks a payment that is out, or confirmed, as Failed.

An input the node reports spent has been taken by some transaction, this one or another. Abandoning over it puts a spent input back into selection and marks the payment Failed while the chain may hold it.
The point of Abandon is that the inputs return to selection. A Failed record whose entries stay in the spent set locks the coins for good, which is the condition Abandon exists to end.
With RequiredConfirmations at zero no intent ever confirms and the spent set only grows. The misconfiguration must be refused rather than run silently.

mutants.replace: record, err := e.reread(ctx, in, StateBroadcast, StateBuilt)
mutants.why: Rebroadcast bypasses the hold check and the reservation because a Broadcast intent's inputs are permanent entries already. A Built intent through it would be sent while held, or without its inputs re-reserved.

An empty 401 read as a body that is not JSON is a transport failure, which at a broadcast is an unknown outcome: every intent stays Built and is re-sent each pass, the alert speaks of a mempool race, and the operator looks in the wrong place for a wrong password.

mutants.find: if e, exists := ss.entries[key]; exists && e.sentByAnother(broadcastTxID, intentID) {
mutants.replace: if e, exists := ss.entries[key]; exists && e.sentByAnother(broadcastTxID, intentID) && false {
mutants.why: An entry that records a send is permanent until the chain confirms it. Writing another withdrawal's send over it attributes the input to the transaction that cannot confirm, and the set then describes the wrong payment as in flight.
Forget is the one call that removes a broadcast entry, for an abandoned withdrawal. Dropping only the reservations leaves the abandoned inputs locked, which is what Abandon exists to end.

A transient error or refused credentials is the node answering without taking the bytes; the mark goes back to what earlier attempts left. Keeping it would hold every intent whose first attempt met a node in warmup, for a rejection that has nothing behind it on the network.
An Abandon whose Forget did not land leaves a Failed record and the entries on disk, and nothing else ever frees those inputs: Recover releases reservations only and Abandon refuses a Failed record.

The placeholder is not a txid. Sent to the node it is an invalid-parameter error on every call, which Abandon returns as it is, so a hold armed without the node's txid would have no exit through the engine.

mutants.find: in.SentAt = sentAt // the node answered and did not take the bytes
mutants.replace: _ = sentAt // the node answered and did not take the bytes
mutants.why: A re-send the node refused reached no peer. Counting it as a send restarts the wait on every pass of a loop that rebroadcasts an unknown transaction, and Abandon is never reachable while the loop runs.
Every save moves UpdatedAt, a refused Rebroadcast included. The wait is about bytes reaching peers, so it is measured from the last send the node did not refuse.

A record written before the mark existed carries attempts whose outcomes are not on record. Reading them as answered lets a rejection fail the intent and release inputs an earlier attempt may have relayed.

mutants.find:
if sentAt.IsZero() {
		sentAt = in.UpdatedAt // a record from before SentAt existed
mutants.replace:
if false {
		sentAt = in.UpdatedAt // a record from before SentAt existed
mutants.why: Putting a zero SentAt back after a refused re-send sends Abandon to UpdatedAt, which the save just moved; a record from the released version that the node forgot is then never abandonable while the loop re-sends it.

mutants.find:
if err := e.save(ctx, in, StateBroadcast); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("record re-send
mutants.replace:
if err := e.save(ctx, in, StateBroadcast); err != nil && false {
		return fmt.Errorf("record re-send
mutants.why: A re-send whose reply is lost and whose save then fails leaves a stale SentAt on disk, and Abandon passes its wait on it a moment after the bytes went to peers.
A Failed intent that was not abandoned and owns broadcast entries is a store that never recorded a send the set did. Dropping the entries frees the inputs of a transaction the node took.
A drop that is not on disk must not take effect in memory: the process would select inputs the file still records as spent, and a restart would put the entries back under a record that says Failed.
